reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: The prototypical task-specific focal hand dystonia, provoked specifically by writing
Abnormal posturing or cramping of the hand and forearm develops shortly after beginning to write and impairs legibility
The same hand performs other manual tasks normally, at least initially, which is the hallmark of task specificity
Classified as simple when confined to writing and dystonic (complex) when other manual tasks become affected
Excessive gripping of the pen with abnormal wrist or finger postures is characteristic
It typically begins in adulthood and may be more frequent in those who write extensively
Some patients adapt by writing with the other hand, which can occasionally develop dystonia in turn
reference.pathophysiology: Writer's cramp reflects maladaptive sensorimotor plasticity and deficient inhibition within the motor system, in which repetitive, highly practised writing drives abnormal cortical reorganisation and blurring of the cortical representation of the fingers. Impaired integration of sensory feedback with motor commands leads to excessive co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles during the specific act of writing, producing the abnormal posture. The task specificity reflects the focal, activity-dependent nature of this reorganisation.
additionalDifferentials: Other task-specific dystonias such as musician's dystonia
Overuse injury, tendinopathy or repetitive strain
Peripheral nerve entrapment such as median or ulnar neuropathy
additionalInvestigations: Observation of the patient writing to characterise the posture and confirm task specificity
Surface electromyography demonstrating co-contraction during writing
Nerve conduction studies to exclude entrapment neuropathy
MRI where a secondary or structural cause is suspected
Copper studies and genetic testing in younger patients or those with additional features
Assessment over time for spread of the dystonia to other tasks
redFlags: Posturing at rest or during many tasks, suggesting generalisation or a secondary cause
Sensory loss, weakness or wasting indicating a neuropathic or compressive lesion
Young onset with other neurological features suggesting an inherited dystonia
Features of Wilson's disease in a younger patient
reference.prognosis: Writer's cramp is usually chronic and spontaneous remission is uncommon; however, it is not dangerous and function can generally be maintained. Botulinum toxin injection tailored to the overactive muscles is the most effective treatment, with adjuncts including writing aids, technique modification and sometimes switching hands. Some patients manage well with practical adaptations alone.
pitfalls: Labelling the problem as psychological or as simple writer's fatigue
Not watching the patient write, which is essential to the diagnosis
Overlooking entrapment neuropathy or a musculoskeletal cause
Assuming the dystonia will remain confined to writing
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice, current edition

management: Botulinum toxin injection tailored to the overactive forearm and hand muscles is the most effective treatment for this task-specific focal dystonia
Adaptive strategies including writing aids, a modified or broadened pen grip, altered posture and switching to typing or voice dictation
Motor retraining, physiotherapy and use of sensory tricks to reduce the abnormal co-contraction
Oral agents such as anticholinergics as adjuncts, recognising their limited and variable benefit
Attention to writing ergonomics and reduction of provoking task load
Neurology referral, with exclusion of a secondary cause including Wilson's disease through copper studies in younger patients or those with additional neurological features
